claims.text: HEAs can provide wear-resistant surface coatings.
A Ni-based interlayer between Cu and an HEA top coating will improve interfacial bonding.
A Ni-containing HEA gradient layer could serve the same bonding function as a Ni-based interlayer.
Improved interfacial bonding will enhance the overall wear resistance of the Cu/interlayer/HEA system.
The initial material is a bare Cu surface intended to receive wear-resistant surface protection.
The Ni-based interlayer can be deposited by sputtering, laser cladding, or a similar process before HEA deposition.
Severe wear, elevated temperature, thermal cycling, and mechanical stress contribute to interface degradation.
The interlayer creates a graded transition from Cu to the HEA coating.
A graded interface reduces interfacial stress and accommodates differences in thermal expansion.
Ni has good mutual solubility with Cu.
Ni has a thermal expansion coefficient closer to that of Cu than the relevant HEA coating does.
Ni–Cu mutual solubility and thermal-expansion compatibility promote metallurgical bonding.
The Ni-based interlayer reduces interfacial stresses that could cause delamination.
Relative to direct HEA deposition on Cu, the Ni-based interlayer will increase adhesion strength and reduce delamination and wear rate.
Direct deposition of the HEA on Cu is expected to produce poorer adhesion and greater delamination under wear than deposition with a Ni-based interlayer.
Extreme service conditions or substantial processing mismatches may compromise the interface despite the interlayer.
Optimal interlayer thickness and composition may depend on the HEA formulation and processing method.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant adhesion increase and wear-rate reduction relative to direct HEA deposition would falsify the hypothesis.
